title: Jehoshaphat Teaches the Law and Grows Strong
summary: Jehoshaphat succeeds Asa, strengthens Judah's defenses, and seeks the God of his father rather than the Baals, and the LORD establishes his kingdom with riches and honor. In his third year he sends officials, Levites, and priests throughout Judah to teach the people from the Book of the Law. The surrounding nations fear the LORD and leave Judah in peace, some bring tribute, and Jehoshaphat builds fortresses and commands a large army.
story: Asa's reign ended in decline (chapter 16). His son Jehoshaphat receives four chapters (17 to 20), more than any king of Judah between Solomon and Hezekiah, and his reign mixes deep faithfulness with a dangerous alliance with the northern king Ahab. This opening chapter is an unmixed picture of blessing. It shows what the Chronicler thinks a good king does: he seeks God, removes idolatry, and puts the word of God in the hands of the people. The next chapter introduces the alliance that will complicate everything.
historical:
Jehoshaphat reigned twenty-five years (20:31), commonly dated to about 872 to 848 BC, with his reign probably overlapping at the start with his father's final years. He was a contemporary of the northern kings Ahab, Ahaziah, and Joram, and of the prophet Elijah. The books of Kings give him a favorable but brief summary (1 Kings 22:41-50) and tell of his joint campaigns with Ahab and Joram (1 Kings 22; 2 Kings 3). The teaching mission of verses 7 to 9 and the military roster of verses 14 to 19 appear only in Chronicles.

Verse 3 says he walked in the earlier ways of his father David. Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek translation lack the name David, which would make the comparison with Asa's earlier, faithful years; either reading fits the Chronicler's view that the early years of a reign often set a standard later abandoned. The Baals were local forms of the Canaanite storm and fertility god Baal, whose worship was being promoted in the north under Ahab and his Phoenician wife Jezebel (1 Kings 16:31-33), which gives weight to the statement that Jehoshaphat did not seek them.
cultural:
The Book of the Law of the LORD that the teachers carried was a scroll containing Israel's law, most likely some form of the law of Moses, perhaps including Deuteronomy. In a world where few people could read and books were copied by hand, a traveling teaching mission was the way the law reached ordinary towns. Deuteronomy had assigned the Levites and priests the task of teaching Israel God's law (Deuteronomy 33:10), and here royal officials join them, so the king's authority stands behind the teaching.

Tribute from Philistines and Arabs reflects the ancient practice by which weaker neighbors sent gifts to a stronger king to keep peace and signal loyalty. The Arabs here were pastoral peoples of the southern and eastern deserts, so their tribute comes in flocks. The long list of personal names (officials, Levites, priests, commanders) is typical of Chronicles and gave its readers a sense of real people and families behind the account. Amasiah is described as one who volunteered himself for the LORD, a phrase that recalls the willing offerings of 1 Chronicles 29.
literary: The chapter alternates between Jehoshaphat's faith and its results in strength. It opens and closes with military preparations (verses 1 and 2, then 12 to 19), and between them stand his seeking of God (verses 3 to 6) and the teaching mission (verses 7 to 9), with the fear of the LORD falling on the nations as the result (verses 10 and 11). The structure makes the teaching of God's law the center that holds everything else together. Verse 6 uses a phrase that elsewhere describes pride, his heart was lifted up, but applies it positively to his courage in the ways of the LORD. The military numbers are the largest assigned to any king of Judah, presenting Jehoshaphat's strength as God's blessing.

outline.t: Jehoshaphat seeks God, and the LORD establishes his kingdom
Officials, Levites, and priests teach the law in Judah's towns
The fear of the LORD on the nations, tribute, and building

doctrines.note: The king sends teachers with the Book of the Law to every town. God's word is meant to be known by the whole people, not kept by an elite, and faithful leadership makes that possible.
Jehoshaphat's refusal to seek the Baals, while the northern kingdom embraced them, is presented as the root of his blessing. He also removed high places and Asherah poles.
The fear of the LORD falling on neighboring kingdoms shows God defending his people when they honor him. Security comes from God's presence as much as from fortresses.

words.note: Lamad, to learn, or in this form, to teach. It is the root of the later word Talmud and is used in Deuteronomy for learning to fear the LORD. It occurs three times in verses 7 to 9, showing the importance the Chronicler gives to this mission.

Torah, instruction or law. It covers commandments but also the broader teaching of God's ways. The Book of the Law of the LORD is the content of the mission, and the Chronicler's readers, who were rebuilding around the Torah after the exile, would have recognized their own priorities here.

Gavah, to be high or lifted up. Usually it describes pride, as with Uzziah in 26:16. In verse 6 it is used positively: Jehoshaphat's heart was lifted up, or took delight, in the ways of the LORD, suggesting courage and zeal rather than arrogance.
Pachad, dread or terror. The dread of the LORD, not of Jehoshaphat, falls on the surrounding kingdoms. The same idea appears in 14:14 and 20:29. It presents God as the real defender of Judah.

christ: Jehoshaphat's teaching mission reflects a longing found across the Old Testament: that God's people would know his law. Jesus spent much of his ministry teaching in the towns of Galilee (Matthew 9:35), and he sent out his disciples to teach what he had commanded (Matthew 28:19-20). The prophets looked forward to a day when all would know the LORD from the least to the greatest (Jeremiah 31:34), and the New Testament sees that fulfilled through the Spirit given to all God's people. The link is thematic rather than predictive.
questions: Jehoshaphat made sure God's word reached every town. What would it take for Scripture to be better known in your home, church, or community?
Verse 6 says his heart took delight in the ways of the LORD. What is the difference between courage in God's ways and pride in your own?
The chapter links the teaching of God's law to peace and strength. How has knowing Scripture well made a practical difference in your life or someone else's?
